item.content:encoded:
Who is OrcaPulse?

We built the agency we wished existed when we were on the client side small, senior, outcome-led, and ruthlessly honest about what actually moves the number.

Our story

How we got here.

Twelve years ago, we were marketers inside the kind of businesses most agencies try to win. We watched good budgets get spent on bad strategy. We watched senior partners sell engagements that juniors delivered. We watched reporting dashboards get prettier while revenue stayed flat.

So we started OrcaPulse with a different brief: a small team of senior operators who do the work themselves, measure the only numbers that matter, and refuse the clients where neither of us would be proud of the outcome.

The result is quieter than most agencies. No sixty-person retreats. No awards wall. Just a short list of clients across the GCC, the US and APAC who stay for years, and a method that gets sharper every quarter it runs.

What we believe

Five principles,
never compromised.

01

Clarity beats cleverness.

The best campaign is the one your mother could explain. We write for comprehension, then make it beautiful never the other way around.

02

Positioning before promotion.

If we can't sharpen what you're selling, no amount of media spend will fix it. Every engagement starts with the thing worth saying.

03

Senior people, every day.

The person who sells you the engagement is the person running it. No account-manager layer, no juniors learning on your budget.

04

Measured in revenue, not reach.

Impressions make reports look busy. Pipeline, LTV and gross margin decide whether we keep the account.

05

Build to compound.

Every quarter should leave you with a cheaper CAC, a deeper moat, or an asset you did not have before.

06

Discretion by default.

Case studies published only with written permission. Many of our best engagements will never appear on this site.

Team

Senior-led, by design.

No account managers between you and the people doing the work. Every engagement is owned by a partner the person who scoped it is the person running it.

Founding Partner

Twelve years leading growth at consumer and B2B brands across the GCC and internationally. Writes most of what you'll see across the business.

Partner Name

Former media buyer at a top-ten regional agency. Runs every paid portfolio across the house.

Partner Name

Partner, Craft

Design and brand lead. Sets the standard every surface the agency ships has to clear.

Ready to grow?

Why is Abu Dhabi more B2B-weighted than Dubai?+

How different are government and sovereign engagements?+

Procurement is slower, more formal, and more credential-driven. Content and PR carry disproportionate weight. Discretion is a service. Pure-performance marketing playbooks don't translate well.

Yes, for finance, energy and professional services. LinkedIn gets a bigger share of attention from decision-makers than any other channel. Instagram is a strong second for consumer, culture and hospitality not B2B.

You can share brand and creative, but the media plan should treat them as separate markets. Audience, platforms, and messaging mix all differ. We run them as linked but distinct in every pan-UAE engagement.

item.content:encoded:
Media mix in Auckland

Channels that work.

Google dominates. Instagram and YouTube drive premium consumer. LinkedIn is central for the local B2B scene. Content and PR carry more weight here than most agencies realise — the market rewards authentic storytelling.

Common questions

About marketing in Auckland.

Why hire a GCC-native agency in Auckland?+

If a meaningful share of your audience is GCC-connected — Gulf HNW tourists, Gulf food buyers, Gulf SaaS prospects — a generalist Auckland agency will not have the depth. We do. For NZ-only audiences, we would recommend a local shop.

Can you handle GCC HNW tourism marketing?+

Yes. Gulf travellers increasingly include NZ (particularly Queenstown and the South Island) in their itineraries. Marketing to them needs Arabic creative, Gulf travel-season understanding, and partnerships with Dubai and Riyadh luxury travel operators.

Do you work with NZ premium food exporters?+

Yes. NZ dairy, lamb, mānuka honey and seafood have strong GCC demand that is routinely marketed badly. The Gulf buyer cares about origin story, provenance, and trust signals — generic export brochures do not move it.

How is NZ different from Australia for marketing?+

Smaller scale, more intimate buyer universe, more content-and-trust-led. CPMs are lower. The country rewards authentic brands and punishes marketing that smells inauthentic. Patience pays better than spend.

What are typical Auckland campaign budgets?+

Lower than most Australian cities. Depends heavily on whether work is NZ-domestic or GCC-facing. On a call we will give you a realistic range.

Manama holds the vast majority of corporate activity and nearly all the fintech infrastructure. Muharraq is growing on the back of aviation, logistics and lower-cost commercial real estate.

Specialise or lose.

Write about regulation.

How Saudi Arabia actually works.

Saudi Arabia is the biggest market in the Gulf by every measure that matters population, GDP, business count, and marketing spend. Vision 2030 is behind the acceleration: giga-projects, tourism infrastructure, fintech regulation, and a serious push to diversify beyond oil.

Riyadh gets most of the enterprise, government and giga-project money. Jeddah gets most of the retail, F&B and hospitality money. The buyer in each city thinks differently, researches differently and buys differently.

A Saudi campaign built from a Dubai playbook will usually underperform. The language is different (Najdi vs Hejazi dialect), the platform mix is different (Snapchat and TikTok dominate here), and the procurement standards are tougher.

Key industries

Where the money is being spent.

01

Giga-projects & real estate

NEOM, Diriyah, Qiddiya, Red Sea Global. Both direct marketing and a supplier ecosystem of agencies, consultants and services.

A category being invented in real time. Payments, BNPL, wealth, Islamic finance, open banking.

03

Entertainment

A sector that barely existed before 2017. Cinemas, concerts, Riyadh Season, sports.

Tourism & hospitality

A new category with new rules. Hotels, DMCs, experiences, religious tourism.

Enterprise B2B

Advisory, legal, cloud, cybersecurity all following the capital flows.

Family groups digitising fast. International brands entering weekly.

How buyers actually make decisions here.

Short-form video first.

TikTok and Instagram Reels drive top-of-funnel for almost every consumer category.

Snapchat still dominant.

Especially for younger Saudi audiences. One of the strongest Snapchat markets in the Arab world.

03

Vernacular Arabic matters.

Marketing in modern-standard Arabic is table stakes. Dialect-aware marketing is the differentiator.

04

LinkedIn is a real B2B channel.

The audience is there and the sophistication is high. Thin posts don't rank.

05

Buyers demand data.

Private firms require clear business cases, ROI tracking and reporting discipline. Generalist agencies struggle to win.

The right approach

How to actually market in Saudi Arabia.

What works, what wastes money, and what we actually do differently.

01

Localise, don't translate.

Hire native copywriters, not translation agencies. Najdi dialect for Riyadh, Hejazi for Jeddah.

02

Snapchat and TikTok on day one.

If your plan is Google + Meta only, you're missing the two biggest attention platforms in the Kingdom.

03

Prove the ROI.

Saudi procurement respects data. Build reporting dashboards from week one and report against revenue, not vanity metrics.

04

Be present.

In-person meetings and relationship-led selling beat remote-only agencies here.

In raw size, yes Saudi Arabia has about 10× the population of the UAE and a marketing market more than twice the size. But the UAE is easier to enter, more open to international brands, and has lower cultural and language barriers.

For anything consumer-facing, yes. For enterprise B2B English-only is survivable but limiting. Even B2B wins are easier if you have Arabic on the ground.

How different is Riyadh from Jeddah for marketing?+

Very. Different dialect (Najdi vs Hejazi), different consumer behaviour, different priority industries, different calendar (religious tourism dominates Jeddah). A single Saudi campaign treating them as one market usually underperforms.

Massive, both directly and indirectly. Direct: a wave of giga-project and government marketing. Indirect: it has reset Saudi buyer expectations about brand quality, digital service, and transparency across every category.

Snapchat and TikTok lead for consumer. Instagram still relevant for premium. YouTube for brand. LinkedIn for B2B. X (Twitter) still used in news and some B2B. Facebook has declined.

Lead with brand.

Pure performance marketing burns cash in the UAE. Buyers choose brands they recognise. Build the brand first, then run performance on top.

The agencies winning here spend as much on production as on paid. Thumb-stopping creative beats thumb-stopping budgets.

Patients research for weeks before choosing a clinic. OrcaPulse helps multi-location dental and aesthetic clinics be the one they trust.

What brings Dental & Aesthetic Clinics businesses here

The real problems we see.

If more than two feel familiar, you're not alone and you're probably paying for them more than you realise.

  • You run paid ads but the leads don't become bookings.
  • Your reviews are good but new patient volume is flat.
  • You can't tell which treatments produce the highest-value patients.
  • Google My Business shows competitors ahead with worse clinics.
  • You're spending on influencers but attribution is a mystery.
  • You know you need patient video content but have no system to produce it.
Who you're trying to reach

The customers behind Dental & Aesthetic Clinics.

Each segment has its own behaviour, platforms and messaging. One campaign doesn't fit all of them.

Segment 01

Aesthetic procedure buyers

Research-heavy, trust-sensitive. Veneers, Botox, fillers, body contouring, hair restoration.

Segment 02

Family dental patients

Repeat-visit, trust-driven, often loyal for years once acquired.

Segment 03

Orthodontic patients (Invisalign, braces)

Longer sales cycle, higher LTV, teen + adult audiences.

Segment 04

Dental tourism patients

International, especially UK, GCC, Europe. Needs full-journey marketing.

Segment 05

Premium / HNW patients

Discretion-sensitive, concierge expectation.

Channels

Where to invest. Where not to.

Not every channel earns a place in a Dental & Aesthetic Clinics plan. Here's where the budget belongs and where it burns.

Where to invest

  • Google Search + Google My Business
    First stop for every patient. Local SEO is non-negotiable.
  • Instagram and TikTok
    Before/after content, patient stories, clinician reels.
  • Snapchat
    Strong in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait for younger aesthetic patients.
  • YouTube Shorts
    Procedure explainers, clinician authority content.
  • Meta paid lead ads with WhatsApp
    The strongest conversion path for most GCC clinics.
  • Review platforms (Google Reviews, Doctify, specialist platforms)
    Trust layer critical for high-ticket procedures.

Where not to

  • LinkedIn for consumer aesthetic
    Wrong audience. B2B channel, not patient channel.
  • Generic brand awareness ads
    Patients want proof, not atmosphere.
  • Programmatic banners
    Burn budget. Rare conversion in a trust-driven category.
  • Pinterest / Reddit
    Minimal patient discovery for most aesthetic categories in GCC.
The campaign shape

What actually converts.

Offer, landing page and messaging the three things most Dental & Aesthetic Clinics campaigns get wrong.

The offer

Clinic offers work best with specific outcomes and transparent pricing. 'Invisalign from AED X free initial consultation' outperforms 'premium orthodontic care'. Finance structures (monthly plans) are major conversion levers for aesthetic and ortho.

The landing page

Procedure-specific pages (not clinic homepage): clinician bio, before/after gallery, price range, finance options, booking form with WhatsApp, FAQs about safety and recovery. Trust signals above the fold.

The follow-up

Decisions take 2–8 weeks for high-ticket aesthetic. A follow-up cadence of personalised WhatsApp messages, educational content, and consultation reminders not just discount pings closes the gap.

What we test
  • Procedure-specific landing pages vs clinic homepage.
  • WhatsApp-first lead capture vs form-fill.
  • Named-clinician creative vs generic clinic creative.
  • Before/after content vs lifestyle content vs educational content.
  • Finance-led vs premium-led positioning.
What we need
  • Procedure portfolio and pricing.
  • Historical lead data by procedure and source.
  • Clinician roster with licensing and specialities.
  • Patient CRM access.
  • Review and reputation data (Google Reviews, Doctify, Trustpilot).
What we measure
  • Qualified consultation bookings per channel.
  • Consultation-to-treatment conversion rate.
  • Average revenue per acquired patient.
  • Patient LTV by procedure type.
  • Review growth rate and sentiment.

01

Treating every procedure the same veneers and family dental have different buyers.

02

Letting leads go cold 48h slow response destroys this category.

03

Generic creative that doesn't show the clinician.

No WhatsApp option losing most GCC patients.

The real questions prospects ask us before signing an engagement.

What's a realistic monthly marketing budget for a clinic?+

Budgets vary widely with clinic scale, procedure mix and city. High-ticket aesthetic and multi-location groups invest more; smaller family practices less. On a 30-minute call we'll suggest a realistic range for your situation.

How do we handle medical advertising rules in GCC?+

DHA, MOH and equivalents regulate what you can show, claim and promise. We work within the rules before-and-after use, claim language, and influencer disclosures all follow current guidelines.

Should we build an in-house content team or outsource?+

Hybrid works best. In-clinic team captures authentic clinician and patient content; we handle production, editing, strategy and distribution. Pure outsourcing feels fake; pure in-house usually can't scale.

What's the single biggest conversion lever?+

Response time + WhatsApp. Clinics that reply within 10 minutes convert leads at 2–3× the rate of 24-hour responders.

How important are Google Reviews?+

Core. Patients read 10+ reviews before booking a high-ticket consultation. A clinic with a 4.8 avg and 400 reviews outcompetes one with a 4.9 and 60 reviews.

Will dental tourism marketing work for us?+

If you have the capacity, pricing, concierge support and credentialing yes. If you don't, campaigns bring the wrong patients and brand damage follows.

The offer

Fintech offers work best when they're product-specific and risk-mitigated. 'Settle merchant payments in 24h free integration review' outperforms 'faster payments'. Pilots, sandboxes and free trials with real support are the strongest conversion mechanisms.

item.content:encoded:
What AEO actually looks like in practice.

A working teardown of how one B2B brand in Riyadh went from invisible to cited across Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT Search.

Feb 2026 9 min read By OrcaPulse
Essay
{ }

Six months ago, our client a Riyadh-based B2B fintech was invisible to AI search engines. Zero citations in Perplexity. Zero visibility in Google AI Overviews. Zero presence in ChatGPT Search answers for any of their category queries.

Today they're cited by name in all three for the top-of-funnel queries that matter. Here's exactly what we did.

What AEO and GEO actually mean

AEO Answer Engine Optimization. Ranking inside tools like Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT Search when a buyer asks a direct question.

GEO Generative Engine Optimization. Being the source LLMs cite when generating answers across the web.

These are not the same as SEO. The signals are related but different. The content format is different. And in the GCC specifically especially in Doha and Riyadh the share of buyer research happening in AI tools has already outgrown what most agencies realise.

The six moves that worked

1. We mapped the questions our buyer actually asks

Not keywords. Questions. Full-sentence, natural-language questions. 'What is the best open banking API in Saudi Arabia for a mid-sized retailer?' not 'open banking API KSA'.

We used three sources: client interviews with their 20 best customers, Reddit and X conversations, and the 'People Also Ask' and 'Related questions' blocks across the AI search tools themselves.

2. We built one page per question

Each page is 1,500–3,000 words, structured as a direct answer up top, followed by the full context. Direct answer first because that's the format AI engines extract.

3. We added rigorous schema

FAQPage schema, Article schema with named author (with a real bio page), Organization schema, Breadcrumbs. All validated. All deployed consistently.

4. We published an llms.txt

At the root of the domain. Listing the key pages, author bios, and the entities we wanted LLM crawlers to understand. Still an emerging standard; now a competitive edge.

5. We built the author's authority

Named author with a real bio, LinkedIn, published work elsewhere. LLM citations correlate with author authority signals even when the user doesn't see the author.

6. We measured relentlessly

Monthly checks across the top 30 target queries in Perplexity, Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT Search. Not just rankings presence, citation phrasing, and whether competitors were being quoted instead of us.

If your schema and FAQ pages aren't right, you are invisible to AI search. Even if you rank #1 in Google.

What we got wrong early

Three things.

First, we wrote content that was too general. 'What is open banking?' is a question. 'What is open banking in Saudi Arabia under Vision 2030?' is a better question for an AEO page targeting our client's actual buyer.

Second, we underweighted structured data. Pretty content without proper schema doesn't earn AI citations. The signal matters as much as the words.

Third, we were slow to add llms.txt. Early movers won't own this forever but owning it in early 2026 was a meaningful advantage.

What this unlocks

Beyond citations, AEO investment compounds into regular SEO. The structured, question-first content ranks well in Google proper. The schema improves rich snippets. The authority signals help the whole domain.

If you're starting from zero

  • Map 20 real questions your buyers ask. Not 20 keywords.
  • Build one page per question, direct answer up top.
  • FAQPage schema on every page. Validated.
  • Named author with a bio page.
  • Publish an llms.txt.
  • Measure monthly across Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT Search.

Six months. Done well, you'll start showing up.

Translated English SEO fails Arabic rankings.

The most common Arabic SEO mistake is translating an English content programme into Arabic and expecting equivalent rankings. It does not work. Arabic search intent is different. Arabic query structure is different. Arabic competitors are different. A translated page competes against pages written for the audience from the start.

What Arabic search actually looks like.

Mixed-language queries are common (Arabic noun + English brand name). Dialect matters — Saudi Arabic, Gulf Arabic and Egyptian Arabic are not the same for search intent. Voice-input is a rising share, and voice queries skew more colloquial. Google's Arabic index is less saturated than its English index in many commercial categories — which is the opportunity.

The content that ranks in Arabic.

Original Arabic writing produced by native-language writers who understand the audience, not translated English. Longer-form content that answers the full query (Arabic searchers often read deeply). Culturally-specific context — Ramadan timing for retail, Hajj logistics for tourism, local regulation for finance. Faster site speed matters more because mobile network conditions vary more.

The technical layer most agencies skip.

Proper right-to-left HTML. Arabic font loading optimised. Schema markup in Arabic where appropriate. hreflang tags set correctly for Arabic vs. English pages. Localised metadata — Arabic title tags, Arabic descriptions, Arabic image alt text. Each one of these is a routine miss.

The compounding advantage of doing it right.

Arabic search traffic in commercial GCC categories is less competed-for than English. A programme that produces excellent native Arabic content ranks faster and holds longer than the English equivalent would in the same category. For brands serving GCC audiences, this is one of the quietest high-ROI moats available.

The death of the generalist agency in the GCC.

Why 'full-service' is a loser's position in 2026 and what the strongest regional operators are doing instead.

Mar 2026 6 min read By OrcaPulse
Essay
¶

If you run an agency in the GCC right now, you are probably being asked for everything. Social, SEO, paid, web, apps, film, PR, maybe even the fit-out for the new office. The temptation is to say yes.

Say yes often enough and you'll build a mid-market agency servicing mid-market clients at mid-market margins. That's a hard business. The agencies pulling away from the pack in 2026 are doing something different.

What premium buyers actually want in 2026

Three things.

Depth over breadth. Procurement teams at Vision 2030 giga-projects, ADGM fintechs and DIFC wealth firms increasingly prefer vertical specialists. Market reports from both KSA and the UAE flag this trend.

Senior-only engagements. The gap between what partners sell and what juniors deliver has become too wide. Buyers notice.

Honest reporting. Dashboards that connect to revenue, not vanity metrics. Private firms in the GCC are getting far better at demanding this and far less patient with agencies that can't produce it.

Why the generalist model stops working at the top

Three reasons.

First, specialists ship better work. An agency that only does fintech content outperforms a generalist on fintech content. The buyer knows this.

Second, generalists have no defensible moat. Everything they do, dozens of others also do. Pricing drifts down.

Third, you cannot be premium and sell every service. Premium is signalled by what you refuse. Cartier doesn't sell phones. McKinsey doesn't do performance ads. Pentagram doesn't do SEO.

Premium is not about doing more. It is about doing one thing so well that nobody else can be considered.

What premium agencies in the GCC are doing instead

  • Vertical specialism. One deep category fintech, hospitality, real estate, luxury, healthcare and refusing engagements outside it.
  • Senior-led teams. No account manager layers. The person who sold the engagement is the person running it.
  • Flat quarterly fees. Not hourly billing. A fee that signals confidence and avoids the scope-of-work gymnastics that destroy trust.
  • Transparent reporting. Revenue, LTV, gross margin reported against the goals agreed in week one, not reshuffled to flatter.
  • Discretion by default. The best engagements never make the case-study page. Buyers who matter are watching.

What this means if you're hiring an agency

Ask the next agency pitching you two questions.

What do you refuse to work on? If the answer is 'nothing', they will dilute whatever they do for you.

Who is actually running my account? If it is not the person pitching, run.

If you're running an agency

Pick the vertical. Decline the engagements that don't fit. Keep the team small and senior. Price with confidence. Report with honesty. Build to compound.

The generalist agency in the GCC isn't dead. It's just permanently mid-market. If that's where you want to be, carry on.

Local SEO per clinic location, treatment-specific landing pages (implants, aligners, cosmetic rather than one "services" page), and relentless reputation management. Clinics that get these three right outcompete those with triple the paid-media budget.

The conversion lever most clinics ignore.

Response time. Clinics that reply to a lead within 10 minutes convert 2-3x the rate of 24-hour responders. WhatsApp beats email for the GCC market. A named receptionist beats a generic contact form. Automation helps but cannot replace the human first touch.

Content that patients actually read.

Procedure explainers written by the clinician, not an SEO freelancer. Before-and-after work shown ethically and within DHA/MOH rules. Patient stories captured in-clinic. Clinic founder content — the dentist, not the brand. Generic "benefits of dental implants" blog content fools no one and ranks for nothing.

What breaks a dental marketing programme.

Marketing a clinic the way a general service business is marketed. Over-reliance on single-channel paid media. Hiring an agency that has never worked in regulated medical marketing. Running the same creative for a family dental practice and an aesthetic specialist. Each of these is fixable; all are routine.

Dubai vs Riyadh: where premium growth budgets are actually going.

Comparable spend, different mandates. A read on where regional CMOs are placing their 2026 bets.

Jan 2026 11 min read By OrcaPulse
Essay
⇌

If you compare the top premium growth budgets in Dubai and Riyadh in 2026, the totals look remarkably similar. What they're being spent on is not.

Dubai: brand first, performance under it

The biggest Dubai budgets we see in 2026 are weighted toward brand, premium creative and content. CPMs are high. Buyers choose brands they recognise. Pure performance marketing burns cash fast here.

Where the money actually goes:

  • Instagram and YouTube production. High-end creative, often shot locally.
  • Content and SEO. Long-form, bilingual, built for both Google and AI search.
  • Performance media. Google, Meta, LinkedIn, TikTok but weighted toward retargeting and consideration, not cold acquisition.
  • Experiential and PR. Events, launches, premium press.

Riyadh: platform-mix and procurement rigour

Riyadh budgets look similar in size but the platform mix is dramatically different. Snapchat and TikTok dominate consumer. LinkedIn is a bigger B2B channel than in Dubai. And procurement discipline is tougher.

Where the money actually goes:

  • Snapchat and TikTok. At campaign level, with dedicated creative not as afterthoughts.
  • Arabic content. Especially vernacular Najdi dialect for Riyadh audiences.
  • LinkedIn B2B. Vision 2030 has created a wave of senior Saudi executives who consume LinkedIn content.
  • Reporting and dashboards. Private firms demand data. The budget for measurement is bigger here than in Dubai.
A Dubai playbook will underperform in Riyadh by 20–40% on paid media, almost by default. The platforms are different, the dialect is different, and the procurement standard is tougher.

Where both cities are converging

Three places.

AI search. Both markets' affluent buyers are early adopters of Perplexity, ChatGPT Search and Google AI Overviews. AEO and GEO infrastructure is becoming table stakes.

Short-form video. Reels and Shorts dominate attention in both markets, even if the specific platform mix differs.

Vertical specialism. Both markets' top procurement teams increasingly prefer vertical specialists over generalists.

Where they're diverging

Three places.

Snapchat weight. Riyadh keeps it. Dubai dialled it down.

Arabic dialect depth. Riyadh demands Najdi; Dubai still works bilingually in modern-standard Arabic.

Procurement format. Riyadh is more formal more RFPs, more detailed scopes, more compliance. Dubai is more flexible more relationship-led, more conversational.

If you're splitting a 2026 budget

  • Treat Dubai and Riyadh as separate campaigns, not one pan-GCC plan with duplicated creative.
  • Expect your Riyadh creative to need Najdi versions, not just translations.
  • Allocate measurably more budget to Snapchat and TikTok on the Saudi side.
  • Build AI-search infrastructure for both.
  • In Dubai, over-invest in creative. In Riyadh, over-invest in reporting.

How we structure the first ninety days of every engagement.

A field guide. The audits we run, the questions we ask, and the first deliverable that decides the next twelve months.

Dec 2025 11 min read By OrcaPulse
Essay
90

Every OrcaPulse engagement starts the same way. Not because we're inflexible because the first ninety days determine the next twelve months, and we've learned the hard way that skipping steps costs everyone later.

Days 1–14: Diagnose

Three audits, run in parallel.

The brand audit

Positioning, narrative, voice, visual identity, website, content. We look at how the brand actually appears in-market not how the brand book says it should appear.

The acquisition audit

Every paid account. Every pixel. Every conversion event. Server-side tracking. Attribution model. Spend by channel. Return by channel. We find the leaks.

The buyer audit

Interviews with 10–20 of the client's best customers. What they searched. What made them decide. What they almost didn't buy because of.

We produce one document at the end of this phase: a diagnostic. Honest, specific, uncomfortable where it has to be. No fluff, no 'opportunities for improvement' hedging.

Days 15–45: Position

The hardest and most important phase. We sharpen the thing worth saying.

This usually means killing two or three positioning claims that have accumulated over the years and don't work any more. Clients find this uncomfortable; everyone finds it necessary.

Deliverables at the end of this phase:

  • A one-page positioning statement the single sentence we build everything else around.
  • A messaging architecture the three to five supporting claims that back it up.
  • Audience segmentation who we are and are not for.
  • A content pillar framework the topics we own, and why.
Most engagements that fail at month twelve failed at week six because the positioning was never sharpened. We refuse to skip this.

Days 46–75: Build

The engine. Depending on scope, this might include:

  • Website updates or rebuild.
  • Schema and AEO/GEO infrastructure.
  • Rebuilt paid accounts with new audience architecture.
  • Initial content and SEO pillar pages.
  • First wave of creative production static, motion, UGC briefs.
  • Reporting dashboards wired to revenue, not just vanity metrics.

By day 75, everything should be in place to run.

Days 76–90: Launch and read

The first 15 days of actual market exposure. We run everything, we don't over-optimise, and we read the data honestly.

At the end of day 90, we produce a second document: the ninety-day read. What's working, what isn't, what we're changing in month four. This document decides whether we keep going as planned or re-cut.

What this doesn't look like

It doesn't look like a Gantt chart with a thousand tasks. It doesn't look like a daily status call. It doesn't look like a different person running each phase.

It looks like a senior team that stays on the engagement from week one to year three. That's the model.

What this costs

A ninety-day diagnostic, position and build engagement runs around $40–120K depending on scope and complexity. This is a flat fee, not an hourly estimate. It covers everything in the three phases above.

Clients who complete it typically stay with us for 18+ months on a quarterly retainer. The ninety days is where that commitment gets earned.

If you're hiring an agency

Ask them how they structure the first ninety days. If the answer is 'we jump straight into execution' walk. The engagements that fail are the ones that skipped diagnosis.

Pricing a premium agency: a defence of flat fees.

Hourly billing is a tax on honesty. Flat quarterly retainers are not a pricing choice they are a positioning choice.

Feb 2026 7 min read By OrcaPulse
Essay
$

Most agencies price by the hour. We don't. Here's why and why it's a positioning decision, not a pricing one.

What's wrong with hourly billing

Three problems.

It punishes efficiency. If we figure something out in two hours that would normally take ten, hourly billing penalises us for being good.

It kills honesty. If a client asks 'how long will this take?', hourly billing creates an incentive to pad the estimate. Over time, that erodes trust.

It makes scope the enemy. Every change becomes a negotiation. Every email about 'quick questions' becomes an awkward conversation about billing hours. The relationship becomes transactional.

What a flat quarterly fee signals

Three things, all deliberate.

Confidence. We know what the engagement will take. We don't need the escape hatch of hourly billing.

Alignment. Our incentive matches yours. We want to work efficiently because that's how we make the engagement sustainable for us.

Discretion. You get to focus on your business, not on counting our hours.

Hourly billing is a tax on honesty. The agencies that bill it most aggressively are usually the least secure.

What we actually charge

We don't publish rate cards. Every engagement is scoped, then priced as a flat quarterly fee. The fee reflects complexity, team seniority, and the scope of what we're committing to.

If an engagement grows, we re-scope and re-price. We don't nickel-and-dime scope changes mid-quarter.

The common objection and why it's wrong

'What if you under-deliver?'

Clients fire us. Thirty-day notice, in every contract. If we're not earning the retainer, the client walks. That's a stronger incentive than any hourly billing structure.

The quiet benefit nobody talks about

Flat fees protect the relationship. Clients who hire us on retainer stop treating us as a vendor. They start treating us as the team. The questions get better. The decisions get faster. The work compounds.

If you're hiring an agency

Ask about the fee structure in the first meeting. If the answer is 'hourly' or 'depends on scope', ask them to walk you through how they handle creep, over-runs and efficiency. Watch the body language. The agencies most defensive about this are usually the ones most dependent on it.

item.dc:creator: orcapulse
item.content:encoded:
The one metric that decides whether a client stays.

Spoiler: it is not ROAS. It is the client's own belief that you understand their business better than their last agency did.

Jan 2026 5 min read By OrcaPulse
Essay
★

Agencies obsess over the wrong retention metric. ROAS, CPL, CAC all useful, none decisive. The metric that actually decides whether a client renews is softer and more important.

The real retention metric

Does the client believe you understand their business better than their last agency did?

That is it. That is the whole metric.

Everything else the dashboards, the reporting, the KPIs is upstream or downstream of that one belief.

How you build that belief

Three things, in order.

Ask harder questions. Most agencies ask about objectives. Great agencies ask about constraints, incentives, politics and the specific moments the client has been burned before. The depth of the questions you ask on week one signals whether you'll ever understand the business.

Report in their language. Not agency language. The client doesn't care about CTR or CPM. They care about whether the sales team is getting leads they can close. Translate everything you report into their internal metrics.

Make the hard call. The agencies clients keep are the ones that tell them when a plan is wrong. Not politely sidestep. Call it. Clients respect agencies that disagree well.

Clients don't renew because you hit the KPI. They renew because they trust you more than they trust the alternative.

How you kill that belief

Three ways.

Juniors doing the work after seniors sold it. The client sees this instantly. The quality shift tells them you don't actually understand their business the person who did has moved on to the next pitch.

Reporting that explains away misses. If your monthly reports always find a way to make a bad month look fine, clients stop reading them. And eventually, they stop trusting you.

Yes-ing bad ideas. The client floats an idea you know is wrong. You agree. It fails. You lose the client twice: once for executing a bad idea, and once for not calling it.

What this means for pricing

Clients who feel understood pay flat quarterly fees without complaint. Clients who feel like a line item argue over every hour. The pricing structure is downstream of whether the client trusts you.

What this means for team structure

Senior-only. Not aspirational operational. The person who understands the client's business has to be the person doing the work. Every account-manager layer is a trust decay. The agencies that keep clients longest keep teams smallest.

What this means for retention

You will know whether a client is renewing six months before the renewal conversation. You will know in the body language on the monthly calls. You will know in how fast they respond to your emails. You will know in which internal meetings they invite you into.

If those signals are good, the renewal is a formality. If they're bad, no last-minute heroics will fix it.

How we collect, use and protect your personal information. Last updated: January 2026.

Who we are

OrcaPulse (“we”, “us”, “our”) is a growth marketing agency. This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use and share information about you when you visit our website or engage us for services.

Information we collect

We collect three types of information:

  • Information you give us. When you book a strategy call, enquire about our services, or email us, we collect the name, email, company, phone number and context you share.
  • Information collected automatically. When you visit the site, we collect standard analytics data: IP address, browser type, pages viewed, time on site, referring source. We use this to understand how the site is used, not to identify you personally.
  • Cookies and similar technologies. We use essential cookies for the site to function and analytics cookies to measure traffic. You can disable non-essential cookies in your browser settings.

How we use information

  • To respond to your enquiry and schedule a call.
  • To deliver services if we enter into an engagement.
  • To send occasional updates about our work (you can unsubscribe at any time).
  • To improve our website and content, in aggregate form.
  • To meet legal and tax obligations.

We do not sell personal information to third parties.

Who we share information with

We share information only with:

  • Service providers that help us run the business (hosting, email, analytics, scheduling). These providers are bound by contract to protect your information.
  • Legal and regulatory authorities where required by law.

Data retention

We keep enquiry information for up to twelve months after your last contact with us. Client engagement data is kept for the duration of the engagement plus seven years for tax and legal purposes, then securely deleted.

Your rights

We operate across the GCC and beyond. Where personal information is transferred outside your country of residence, we rely on standard contractual clauses and appropriate safeguards to protect it.

Security

Our site and services are not directed at children under 16. We do not knowingly collect information from them.

We may update this policy from time to time. The “last updated” date at the top will reflect the most recent revision. Material changes will be flagged on the site.

Looking for a specialist branding and design agency?

An identity that makes every surface recognisable. OrcaPulse builds brand strategy, identity systems and operating guidelines for ambitious brands worldwide.

All services
Wireframe final asset to be added
What usually brings people to us

The real reasons businesses contact us about Brand & Design.

If more than two of these feel familiar, it's probably time to talk.

  • Your brand looks different on every surface.
  • Each designer who touches your brand reinvents it slightly.
  • Your logo is fine but the system around it is a mess.
  • You have brand guidelines but nobody follows them.
  • You're mid-raise, mid-scale, mid-rebrand and the current brand is holding you back.
  • You can't tell your mother what you do in a sentence.
What this service actually is

What we do, in one paragraph.

We handle positioning, identity design (logo, type, color, mark), the full system (components, templates, voice), and the documentation your team actually uses.

Who it's for & when it works

Honest about fit.

Not everyone should buy this. Here's who it works for and when we'd tell you to spend the money differently.

Right fit when

  • You have real reason to rebrand not just boredom with the current one.
  • You can give us access to your customers, team and competitors for research.
  • You can commit 8–14 weeks to the process.
  • You're willing to make hard positioning calls.
  • You trust that strategy and design are not separate.

Wrong fit when

  • You just want a new logo.
  • You expect the full rebrand in 3 weeks.
  • You have no clear reason the current brand isn't working.
  • You need the committee's unanimous approval on every decision.
  • You believe strategy is unnecessary if the design looks nice.
The customer journey

The funnel, in plain words.

TOFU, MOFU, BOFU not jargon. Just where in the journey a buyer is, and what Brand & Design does at each stage.

TOFU
Reach the right people with a mark they recognise.
Identity across every surface ads, social, email, print, environmental. Consistent at a glance.
MOFU
Build interest with a brand that proves depth.
Narrative and messaging architecture that explains what makes you different.
BOFU
Give qualified prospects a clear reason to trust.
Visual and verbal consistency that reads premium. Guidelines your team can actually follow.
Workflow

How we actually run this.

1
Discover
Audience interviews, competitor teardown, archaeological review of existing brand.
2
Define
Positioning, narrative, personality. Written down.
3
Design
Identity system logo, type, color, voice, motion. Tested in real contexts.
4
Document
Guidelines that are usable. A 40-page manual an in-house designer can actually follow.
5
Deploy
Rollout across priority touchpoints site, social, decks, email.
6
Steward
Quarterly check-ins to prevent drift as the business scales.
Platforms & channels

Where this gets executed.

Not every channel for every client. We pick based on your market, buyer and goal.

Figma
Design system, components, specs.
Website / app surfaces
Where the brand lives most.
Social and ads
Where the brand gets tested daily.
Print and environmental
Business cards, signage, retail, packaging.
Pitch decks and sales materials
Where the brand converts.
Internal docs and email
Where the brand drifts fastest if it isn't operationalised.
Getting started

The first 30 days.

Three things happen when we start: we identify the tests, gather the data, and set expectations against a realistic timeline.

What we test
  • Positioning statement the one sentence everything else is built from.
  • Logo stress-test small sizes, dark/light, bad backgrounds.
  • Type system headline + body + accent, tested across content.
  • Color system in context, not on a dieline.
  • Voice test same message, written three different ways, which feels right.
What we need from you
  • Current brand assets (logo files, color codes, type specs).
  • Access to existing customers for interviews.
  • Competitor list for teardown.
  • Product / service portfolio and roadmap.
  • Business goals (next 2–3 years).
What to expect
Weeks 1–2
Research interviews, teardowns, archaeological review.
Weeks 3–5
Positioning, narrative, personality. First visual directions.
Weeks 6–9
Identity design logo, type, color. Design system foundations.
Weeks 10–12
Guidelines documented. Rollout plan agreed.
Months 4+
Steward retainer quarterly check-ins, drift prevention.

What goes wrong

The common mistakes.

The patterns we see repeated across underperforming programs. Fix any of these and performance usually moves immediately.

01

Starting with the logo.

Positioning first. The logo is the last 10% of the project, not the first.

02

Skipping the audit of what works.

Equity exists. Changing too much destroys it.

03

Designing in isolation.

Logos look great on a dieline. The real test is email, pitch deck, Instagram story.

04

Writing aspirational guidelines.

Guidelines nobody uses are worse than no guidelines. Write for the designer who's never read the brand book.

What good looks like

How we measure and scale.

The metrics we track, and what we do once we have a winner.

We measure
  • Consistency score across surfaces (audited quarterly).
  • Brand recall in buyer research.
  • Qualified lead quality lift post-rebrand.
  • Sales cycle shortening (clearer brand = faster buyer decisions).
  • Partnership and PR inbound increase.
Then we scale
  1. 01Roll the system out across remaining surfaces in sequence.
  2. 02Train the in-house team on guidelines.
  3. 03Steward quarterly audit drift, update components, extend into new categories.
  4. 04Open the system up to partners and licensees (where relevant).
Questions, answered

Common questions.

The real questions prospects ask us before signing an engagement.

How long does a brand project take?+

8–14 weeks for most engagements, depending on scope and research depth. Rush timelines are possible but produce worse work.

Rebrand or new brand?+

Both. For rebrands, we audit what equity exists before touching it. Most brands lose more by changing too much than by changing too little.

Strategy without design?+

Yes. We write the positioning, narrative and personality document. Your existing design team or another agency can execute.

What size organisations do you work with?+

Founder-led startups preparing to raise through mid-market businesses rebranding at $20–200M revenue.

Will the logo change?+

Sometimes. Often not. We evaluate equity first. If the current logo is working, we modernise rather than replace.

How do you handle Arabic typography?+

We work with Arabic type specialists on every brand with a GCC audience. The RTL + LTR system is designed in parallel, not an afterthought.

What's a steward retainer?+

A small quarterly engagement where we audit how the brand is being used, update components as needed, and prevent the drift that undoes most rebrands.

We take on a limited number of partnerships each quarter. Thirty minutes, no pitch a frank conversation about where your growth is leaking and what it would take to seal it.

Who it's for & when it works

Honest about fit.

  • You have deep expertise that competitors don't.
  • You're willing to say something, not just publish updates.
  • Your sales cycle is long enough that content matters.
  • You can wait 6 months for compounding results.

Build interest with depth that competitors can't match.

Strategise
Pillars, voice, questions worth owning.
2
Research
Primary interviews, data pulls, competitor dissection.
3
Produce
Written by humans with domain depth. Edited to a house standard.
4
Publish
Properly formatted, imaged, schema-tagged.
5
Distribute
SEO, newsletter, social, syndication. Nothing published and forgotten.
6
Measure
Monthly reporting on traffic, newsletter growth, qualified leads, sales attribution.

The compounding asset. Where everything else routes to.

Guest posts, syndication, named author credits.

Long-form audio and video expanding the content asset.

For brands building audience, not just customers.

  • Pillar topic selection the 3–5 topics you can realistically own.
  • Author voice test ghostwriting a founder piece vs their own voice.
  • Format test long-form essay vs structured guide vs case study.
  • Newsletter cadence weekly vs biweekly vs monthly.
  • Distribution channel which platform amplifies the piece best.

First publication cycle live. Newsletter cadence in place.

First rankings and newsletter growth measurable.

Content becomes a self-sustaining acquisition channel.

The patterns we see repeated across underperforming programs. Fix any of these and performance usually moves immediately.

01

Using AI to write finished copy.

Google down-ranks it. Buyers notice. Your brand voice erodes.

02

Publishing without a plan to promote.

Great writing with no distribution is a journal, not a strategy.

03

Writing for 'everyone' and reaching no one.

Specificity wins. Niche audiences compound faster than broad ones.

04

Letting content and SEO work in silos.

Content without entities + schema is content that doesn't rank.

  • Organic traffic to published content.

How many pieces per month?+

Quality over cadence. Typically 2–6 long-form pieces monthly, plus a weekly newsletter and supporting shorter content.

Yes one of our most-requested services. We interview, draft, and iterate until the voice is unmistakably theirs.

How long is a 'long-form' piece?+

Usually 1,500–4,000 words, depending on topic and intent. Shorter when the question is specific. Longer when the piece is a definitive resource.

We can set up house editorial under a brand name, or named-author programs for several team members, or a mix. We'll recommend what fits your buyer.

Native Arabic writers for both MSA and dialect. Research and editorial standards are the same across languages.

Different grammar. Different pacing. Different hooks. It never works.

Burning the budget on one hero asset.

Modern campaigns need 10+ variants per concept. One beautiful film ≠ a campaign.

Not shooting for the edit.

Days are expensive. Shoot a shot list the edit needs, not everything that looks nice.

Ignoring sound design.

Vertical social video with weak audio bombs. Sound is half the craft.

What goes wrong

The common mistakes.

The patterns we see repeated across underperforming programs. Fix any of these and performance usually moves immediately.

01

Posting the same creative on every platform.

Reels aren't LinkedIn posts aren't TikToks. Platform-native content wins.

02

Letting the brand voice drift.

Three different writers = three different brands. Needs one editor.

03

Chasing virality instead of consistency.

One viral post gets you an audience that leaves. Consistency builds one that stays.

04

Ignoring DMs.

Social is a sales channel. DMs that go cold cost deals.

  2. 02Expand into new platforms when the audience justifies it.
  3. 03Build creator partnership programs not one-off deals.
  4. 04Launch content series that run for 6+ months.

How many posts a week should we expect?+

Depends on platform and audience. Typically 3–5 posts per week on Instagram, 3+ on TikTok, 2–3 on LinkedIn. A cadence that fits the brand not a padded calendar.

Our team. In-house creators. We can also work with your in-house team or trusted collaborators.

We reconcile platform-reported metrics against your real conversion data every month. If a channel looks good on the platform but doesn't produce revenue, we flag it.

What about crisis management?+

We have an escalation playbook that activates within an hour. Response protocols, approval chains, and a holding statement framework ready to go.

Looking for a specialist web and e-commerce agency?

Sites that convert and still look like your brand. OrcaPulse builds marketing sites, e-commerce and SaaS platforms for brands working globally.

All services
Wireframe final asset to be added
What usually brings people to us

The real reasons businesses contact us about Web & Commerce.

If more than two of these feel familiar, it's probably time to talk.

  • Your site looks premium but doesn't convert.
  • Your Core Web Vitals are red, your SEO is suffering.
  • Every content edit requires a developer because the CMS is broken.
  • A page builder like Elementor or Divi has made the site slow and unmaintainable.
  • Your checkout, booking or signup flow leaks users at every step.
  • The site your team ships today looks nothing like the brand guidelines.
What this service actually is

What we do, in one paragraph.

We take you from brief to live site. Strategy, UX, design, development, CMS setup, performance, accessibility, SEO, analytics the whole stack as one team.

Who it's for & when it works

Honest about fit.

Not everyone should buy this. Here's who it works for and when we'd tell you to spend the money differently.

Right fit when

  • You know the single number this site needs to move.
  • You have the imagery, copy direction and brand assets ready (or trust us to produce them).
  • You're willing to use a lean CMS instead of a page builder.
  • You understand that performance = SEO = revenue.
  • You want a site that compounds, not one that goes stale in 18 months.

Wrong fit when

  • You want to build the whole thing yourself with Wix.
  • You expect a 6-figure site in a 2-week timeline.
  • You need Elementor or Divi for internal reasons.
  • You have no clear buyer journey.
  • You expect the site to fix a positioning problem.
The customer journey

The funnel, in plain words.

TOFU, MOFU, BOFU not jargon. Just where in the journey a buyer is, and what Web & Commerce does at each stage.

TOFU
Reach the right people on the right page.
SEO-optimised pages built for buyer intent. Social and paid campaigns landing on dedicated conversion pages, not the homepage.
MOFU
Build interest with design, content and proof.
Clear positioning, honest content, visible proof case studies, testimonials, pricing where relevant.
BOFU
Give qualified prospects a clear reason to act.
One primary CTA per page. Fast, friction-free forms, checkouts, bookings. Zero dark patterns.
Workflow

How we actually run this.

1
Strategy
Audience, intent, funnel, and the single number the site has to move.
2
Design
A design system not a stack of pages. Every page uses the same vocabulary.
3
Build
Hand-coded templates on a tight CMS. No builders. No marketplace themes.
4
QA
Core Web Vitals green. Accessibility compliant. SEO preserved from any migration.
5
Launch
Redirects mapped, analytics live, forms tested, team trained.
6
Iterate
Monthly conversion improvements. The site compounds.
Platforms & channels

Where this gets executed.

Not every channel for every client. We pick based on your market, buyer and goal.

WordPress + ACF Pro
For marketing sites and content-heavy builds. Owned infrastructure.
Shopify
For most e-commerce. Shopify + headless for scale.
Framer
For brand-first marketing sites with no deep CMS needs.
Webflow
For design-heavy content sites where visual edits matter.
Headless (Next.js + Payload / Sanity)
For complex, performance-critical or multi-site setups.
Custom Node / Rails / Django
For SaaS platforms with real app logic.
Getting started

The first 30 days.

Three things happen when we start: we identify the tests, gather the data, and set expectations against a realistic timeline.

What we test
  • Core Web Vitals baseline (desktop + mobile).
  • Form and funnel conversion rate on existing site.
  • Heatmap and session recording review (Hotjar, Clarity).
  • Content audit which pages drive leads, which don't.
  • Mobile audit real device testing, not just emulators.
What we need from you
  • Analytics access (GA4) with at least 6 months of history.
  • Google Search Console access.
  • Existing content inventory + brand assets.
  • CRM or form submission data (where leads come from).
  • Full access to current CMS (export + admin).
What to expect
Weeks 1–2
Discovery and strategy. UX wireframes. Content plan.
Weeks 3–6
Design system + high-fidelity pages. CMS architecture agreed.
Weeks 7–10
Development. Content loaded. Analytics wired.
Weeks 11–12
QA, performance, accessibility, launch. Team training.
Month 4+
Monthly CRO retainer. 10–30% conversion lift typical in year one.

What goes wrong

The common mistakes.

The patterns we see repeated across underperforming programs. Fix any of these and performance usually moves immediately.

01

Using a page builder to save money.

Elementor and Divi add 1–3 MB of unused CSS/JS per page. Performance, SEO and maintainability all suffer.

02

Picking a marketplace theme to save time.

Bloat and lock-in. The theme shapes the site more than the brand.

03

No design system.

Every page diverges. Updates take 10× longer. Brand consistency drifts.

04

Ignoring performance.

Core Web Vitals are a Google ranking factor. Slow sites convert worse. Period.

What good looks like

How we measure and scale.

The metrics we track, and what we do once we have a winner.

We measure
  • Core Web Vitals (LCP < 2.0s, CLS < 0.05, INP < 150ms).
  • Conversion rate per page type (home, services, product, blog).
  • Form completion rate.
  • Time to key action (click to book, click to buy).
  • Organic traffic retained post-migration.
Then we scale
  1. 01A/B test the top-3 highest-traffic pages monthly.
  2. 02Add new page templates as new buyer segments emerge.
  3. 03Expand content clusters that are driving organic leads.
  4. 04Replace underperforming CTAs and forms.
Questions, answered

Common questions.

The real questions prospects ask us before signing an engagement.

Why don't you use page builders?+

They destroy performance. The average Elementor or Divi page ships 2–3 MB of unused CSS/JS. Fast, clean, hand-coded templates beat them on every metric.

Can you work with my existing WordPress site?+

Yes. We audit it, usually recommend a lean theme replacement, migrate content and redirects cleanly, and improve performance. Not every project needs a full rebuild.

How long does a build take?+

A focused marketing site: 6–10 weeks. Full commerce or SaaS: 10–16 weeks. We give you a scoped timeline before you commit.

Do you handle ongoing maintenance?+

Yes. Small monthly retainer that covers security, uptime, backups, performance monitoring and small CRO improvements.

What about Shopify vs headless?+

Default to native Shopify for most e-commerce. Go headless (Shopify + Next.js) when the brand demands editorial-grade design, or when you need true app-grade performance.

Can you set up multilingual (English + Arabic)?+

Yes. Full RTL support, Arabic typography, and multi-market content governance built in.

What CMS will I actually use?+

WordPress + ACF Pro for marketing sites form-based editing. Shopify for commerce standard admin. Framer for brand sites visual editor. We train your team on whichever we deploy.
